title: The Network Panel
subtitle: Inspecting HTTP requests, headers, timing, and responses
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Developers cannot debug what they cannot see. Network failures, slow responses, missing headers, and CORS errors are invisible without the Network panel.
whyItExists.solution: The Network panel is a real-time HTTP inspector built into every browser. It shows every request the page makes — URL, method, status code, request headers, response headers, response body, and timing.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Debugging a failed API call, diagnosing a slow page load, checking if CORS headers are present, verifying authentication headers are being sent, inspecting response bodies.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: The Network panel only shows requests made by the current page in the current tab. It does not show server-to-server requests or background processes.

explainModes.beginner: The Network panel is like a phone tap for your browser. Every time the page calls a server — to get data, load an image, or run a script — it shows up here. You can see exactly what was sent and what came back. When your API call fails, the Network panel shows you the exact error message the server returned.
explainModes.simple: Open Network panel → reload the page → see all requests. Each row is one HTTP request. Click a row to see: Headers tab (request/response headers), Preview tab (formatted response), Response tab (raw response body), Timing tab (DNS/TCP/request/response breakdown). Filter by 'Fetch/XHR' to see only API calls. Sort by Size to find large assets. Sort by Time to find slow requests.
explainModes.standard: The Network panel uses the browser's Resource Timing API and the underlying DevTools protocol to capture detailed timing for each request. The waterfall chart shows how requests overlap — HTTP/2 requests can interleave, HTTP/1.1 requests queue. The 'Initiator' column shows which code triggered the request. 'Copy as cURL' (right-click a request) lets you replay a request in the terminal with the exact same headers.
explainModes.technical: The Network panel captures all resource types: Document (HTML), Stylesheet, Script, Image, Font, XHR/Fetch (API calls), WebSocket, Media. The Timing tab breaks each request into: Queueing (waiting for a free connection slot), Stalled (blocked), DNS Lookup, Initial connection (TCP), SSL (TLS handshake), Request sent, Waiting (TTFB — time to first byte), Content download. Long TTFB means slow server processing. Long Content download means large payload or slow connection.
explainModes.deepDive: The Network panel's HAR (HTTP Archive) export format captures a complete session including all timing, headers, and bodies. HAR files are used by performance analysis tools like WebPageTest and GTmetrix. The 'Preserve log' checkbox keeps requests across navigations — useful for debugging redirect chains. 'Throttling' lets you simulate 3G or slower connections to test performance on mobile. Chrome's Priority column shows which requests the browser considered high-priority (HTML, CSS, fonts) vs low-priority (off-screen images, analytics).

content.text: Open DevTools (F12), click the Network tab, then reload the page. Every request the page makes appears as a row.

content.code:
Name        — Filename or URL of the resource
Status      — HTTP status code (200, 404, 500, etc.)
Type        — Resource type (document, fetch, script, img, font)
Initiator   — What triggered this request (HTML parser, JS code, CSS)
Size        — Response size (compressed + uncompressed)
Time        — Total request duration (from send to last byte)
Waterfall   — Visual timing bar showing when the request happened

content.text: Click any row to see the full details of that request and response:

items: Headers tab — Request headers (what you sent) and Response headers (what the server sent back). Check here for Authorization, Content-Type, CORS headers, and Cache-Control.
Preview tab — Pretty-printed response body. JSON is interactive, HTML is rendered, images show visually.
Response tab — Raw response body as text.
Timing tab — Breakdown: DNS, TCP, TLS, Waiting (TTFB), Content download. Long TTFB = slow server. Long Download = large payload.
Cookies tab — Cookies sent in the request and set in the response.

content.code:
Type filter buttons (above the request list):
  All        → Show everything
  Fetch/XHR  → Show only API calls (most useful for debugging APIs)
  JS         → JavaScript files
  CSS        → Stylesheet files
  Img        → Images
  Font       → Font files
  Doc        → HTML documents

Search box filters:
  'api'        → Requests with 'api' in the URL
  '-status:200' → Requests that did NOT return 200
  'larger-than:100k' → Responses over 100KB

content.text: Check Disable cache (checkbox in the toolbar) while developing so you always get fresh responses. Uncheck it when testing caching behavior. Also check Preserve log to keep requests visible across page navigations — useful for debugging redirects.

questions.question: An API call is failing with a red row in the Network panel. What tab in the request details should you check first?
options: Timing — to see how slow it was
Preview or Response — to see the error message the server returned
Cookies — to check for expired cookies
Initiator — to see which line of code made the request
questions.explanation: When an API call fails, the most important thing is to see what the server said. Open the failing request → Preview tab (for formatted JSON) or Response tab (for raw text). The response body almost always contains an error message with the specific reason the request failed — far more useful than just knowing the status code.

questions.question: You load a page and see 80 requests in the Network panel. Which filter shows you only API calls?
questions.explanation: Fetch/XHR filters to requests made by the Fetch API or XMLHttpRequest — which is how JavaScript makes API calls. 'Doc' shows HTML documents. 'JS' shows script files. 'Media' shows video/audio. For debugging API calls, always filter to Fetch/XHR first to reduce noise.

faq.q: Why do I see (from disk cache) or (from memory cache) in the Network panel?
faq.a: These mean the browser used a cached copy instead of making a network request. 'From disk cache' — the response was saved to disk from a previous visit and the Cache-Control headers allow reuse. 'From memory cache' — the response is in RAM, available until the tab closes. These are good for performance — it means the user did not have to wait for a network request.

faq.q: How do I replay a request in the terminal?
faq.a: Right-click any request in the Network panel → Copy → Copy as cURL. Paste the result in your terminal. This gives you the exact same request (same URL, same headers, same body) that the browser sent. You can then modify it with curl flags to test variations.

examples: When a login does not work, check Network → the POST /login request → Response tab — it often says 'Invalid password' or 'Account locked'
When a page is slow, sort Network by Time column to find the slowest request — often a large image or an uncached API call
When you get a CORS error, check the failing request's Response Headers — if Access-Control-Allow-Origin is missing, the server is not configured for CORS
